text:
**Short answer:** about 200 W of solar refills a 1,000 Wh power station in roughly 1.5 days of decent sun. For a full recharge in one day, plan on about 300 to 350 W.

**The math**

Daily energy ≈ panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.7 to 0.75. The 0.7 to 0.75 factor covers heat, panel angle, and charging losses ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/), [Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge)).

| Panel | Approx. energy per day (4.5 sun hours, 70%) | Time to refill 1,000 Wh from empty |
|---|---|---|
| 100 W | ~315 Wh | ~3 days |
| 200 W | ~630 Wh | ~1.5 days |
| 400 W | ~1,260 Wh | Under 1 day |

Source: [Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/).

**Panel watts for a one-day recharge, by sunlight**

- 3 peak sun hours: ~450 W
- 4 peak sun hours: ~340 W
- 5 peak sun hours: ~270 W
- 6 peak sun hours: ~230 W

Source: [Power Runtime](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/). Held in Reserve gives a similar range: about 300 W in summer and 700 W or more in a northern winter ([Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/)).

**Before you buy**

- **Solar input limit:** Your station caps how many watts it accepts. Panels above that limit add nothing, so check the spec sheet. Mid-range 1,000 to 1,500 Wh units typically allow 400 to 800 W, but some cap at 200 W.
- **Voltage:** The panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc) must stay inside the station's input window. Going over can damage the charge controller. Wiring panels in series adds their voltages together.
- **Running loads:** If you draw power while charging, subtract that from the solar input. A fridge averaging 60 W cuts a 200 W input to about 140 W net.
- **Peak sun hours:** These are not daylight hours. Most of the US gets about 3 to 6 per day. Plan around your worst month.
